#38460. Tech Report: Brighton and Crystal Palace: the rise of a rivalry separated by 39 miles

📅 26 Feb 2023 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3356 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Brighton and Crystal Palace: the rise of a rivalry separated by 39 miles

📅 26 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many bands have penned odes to their hometowns over time, singing the praises of their local streets and parks.
  • However, when one considers David Bowie and his recollections of days gone by, it is safe to say that he did not enjoy such wistful memories.
  • According to recent reports, A touch harsh perhaps, but back in the 1970s and 1980s, Croydon did have a reputation as a concrete monstrosity, driven by London banning skyscrapers in the 1960s after which developers had to find somewhere to pour their concrete.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many bands have penned odes to their hometowns over time, singing the praises of their local streets and parks. The Beatles waxed lyrical over Penny Lane and Strawberry Fields; The Kinks invited us to enjoy a Waterloo Sunset; while Gerry Rafferty took his saxophone to Baker Street. Each song echoed memories of great days and blissful childhoods.

However, when one considers David Bowie and his recollections of days gone by, it is safe to say that he did not enjoy such wistful memories. When asked about how he would describe something dreary, he could only think of one place that summed it up for him: “It represented everything I didn’t want in my life, everything I wanted to get away from. I think it’s the most derogatory thing I can say about something: ‘God, it’s so fucking Croydon.”.

According to recent reports, A touch harsh perhaps, but back in the 1970s and 1980s, Croydon did have a reputation as a concrete monstrosity, driven by London banning skyscrapers in the 1960s after which developers had to find somewhere to pour their concrete. And hence the world of architecture was treated to such horrors as the Whitgift Centre, the NLA Tower, an underpass and a flyover.

Sources indicate that oh, and if you think I am being unfair on Croydon town centre, I am speaking from a position of knowledge: I had to spend the first 16 years of my life meeting friends in the Whitgift Centre as the highlight after school. Trust me, the many ways to use concrete were richly celebrated there.

But there did exist an escape route from the London suburb into pastures greener. On a sunny day, it was possible to pack the family up into a Ford Cortina and head off due south down the A23 across the scenic Sussex Downs until land ran out and you were in Brighton. In fact, the road was nicknamed the “Brighton Road” by locals.

Sources indicate that many a school trip was spent going down to that glorious seaside town, enjoying the delights of the pier, drinking too many fizzy drinks and then regretting it on the many fairground rides. A place of fine Victorian architecture, ice creams and sticks of rock. The yin to Croydon’s yang.

Industry observers note that but the drive took a while. Croydon and Brighton are separated by 39 miles; even by train it takes almost an hour from East Croydon to Brighton. Again, I talk from experience having once fallen asleep travelling from Victoria to East Croydon and waking at 1am in Brighton – but let’s not get into that. The point is that the two cities are hardly next door and so really should have no reason to notice the other in any significant way.

According to recent reports, it means that the football teams that exist in both towns, Crystal Palace and Brighton & Hove Albion, both have closer neighbours to concern themselves with. Palace especially, being in south London, have Wimbledon, Charlton and Millwall in their immediate vicinity, not to mention numerous possible other London derbies.

Brighton, meanwhile, are a little more isolated but Portsmouth is 42 miles away – similar to Croydon – and represents another south coast location. And so there should be no real rivalry, and certainly not enough for it to be called a derby in the same way as Liverpool and Everton or Manchester United and City.

Recent findings suggest that fans of both Palace and Brighton will happily tell you that it is not a derby in the true sense of the word, but a rivalry it most definitely is. For the reason why such a strange feud exists, one must go back to Tottenham in the 1960s.

According to recent reports, spurs during that time had a competent team, one that won the FA Cup in 1967, defeating rivals Chelsea 2-1. Playing alongside each other for Spurs on that day were two English midfielders, Alan Mullery and Terry Venables. While both played most of their days together at Tottenham, it wasn’t always a harmonious relationship, with Venables having to be second-in-command to Mullery as captain. They were not best of friends and so when both hung up their boots and started managerial careers, any future meetings between the two had the potential for sparks. And it wouldn’t be long before they would come face-to-face as rivals.

The story moves on to 1970s. For many years, Palace and Brighton hadn’t even been in the same division together. That all changed during the 1974/75 season when they met in the third tier. Brighton had just gone through the short spell of leadership under Brian Clough who, having moved on to his ill-fated time at Leeds, had split with long-time partner Peter Taylor, who took over the reins.

At Palace, meanwhile, the colourful Malcolm Allison was in charge – a man to whom the words humility and shyness most definitely did not apply.

Industry observers note that the game at Brighton’s Goldstone Ground saw a higher-than-usual attendance and resulted in police arrests due to fighting between fans after reports of heavy drinking. The next season saw both teams fighting for promotion, which obviously heightened tensions somewhat, and the game at Selhurst Park saw Palace win 1-0 in front of their largest crowd for two years, despite what Allison described after as an overly physical approach from Brighton.

In a recent development, it is Allison who brings us nicely onto the theme of club nicknames. Until 1973, Crystal Palace had been known as The Glaziers in reference to the famous glass palace after which they are named. But Allison felt that this was not sexy enough, and so after glancing around Europe’s greatest sides and noting that Benfica were The Eagles, the nickname was changed to just that. Hence, a latest terrace chant was born.

Industry observers note that brighton were known as The Dolphins, a name voted on by locals and reflecting the opening of a local Dolphinarium in 1969. But “Come on you Dolphins” just lacked a certain something. Therefore, when the sides met in 1976, a group of Brighton fans decided to answer Palace’s chants with “Come on you Seagulls” – a reference to their fine seaside setting. It was popular and soon became the official nickname, resulting in a fire sale of dolphin-themed merchandise on the south coast.

So now, Eagles vs Seagulls existed as a thing. But having rhyming birds as mascots hardly makes a rivalry. The game that saw the birth of the Seagulls also saw the game almost abandoned due to Palace fans throwing smoke bombs and other missiles onto the pitch. There was something starting to rumble.

1976 saw both sides eventually miss out on promotion, and both subsequently saw a change of management. Palace promoted Venables from coach following Allison’s resignation while Brighton gave Mullery his first managerial post. As such, promotion from the Third Division was a priority for both.

Sources indicate that despite their playing careers being well in the rear-view mirror, there was a simmering tension between the two ex-Spurs men, and their first meeting would occur at the Goldstone Ground, a game once again interrupted three times by smoke bombs. As if to add fuel to the fire, they drew each other in the first round of the FA Cup. The famous tale of ‘Challis of the Palace’ came into existence.

According to recent reports, the initial tie was a draw, with Mullery complaining about Palace’s negative tactics, and the replay also drew a stalemate. As was the case in those days, a second replay was scheduled – and then postponed twice for weather before finally occurring at Stamford Bridge in early December – raising the tension. The Eagles took an early lead, which was then followed by a disallowed goal for Brighton when Peter Ward was adjudged to have handled. After the game, Jim Cannon admitted pushing Ward into the ball to cause the handball.

According to recent reports, and then came the moment that still lives in infamy between both sets of supporters. The Seagulls were awarded a penalty by referee Ron Challis after 78 minutes. Brian Horton converted but, to his astonishment, was forced to retake after Challis adjudged that a Brighton player had encroached, the player protesting that he had been pushed into the area by a Palace man. The second attempt was saved and Brighton ended up exiting the cup. Mullery was not best pleased.

Angry, he had to be escorted off the pitch by police while being heckled by Palace fans. According to his recollection, “A chap there [in the stands], I’d like to meet him again actually, he was up there and he poured a hot coffee all over my head. Literally I had about 30p in my pocket and looked up and stated that’s about all you’re worth.”.

It has been revealed that finally losing his cool, he flicked V-signs at them, swearing at the same time, in an image that is famously revered by Brighton fans still to this day. The gesture ended up costing him more than 30p when the FA slapped him with a £100 fine.

Sources indicate that the season ended on a high for both teams as they achieved promotion to Division Two, meaning that the simmering rivalry would continue. And both were on a roll: the 1978/79 campaign saw both clubs promoted together once again, this time to the big time, with Palace snatching the title from Brighton in their final match. Their destinies seemed entwined at this time and it is really this whole period which created what some now call the A23 derby.

Since then, the rivalry has seen many infamous moments. 1982 saw Mullery appointed as Crystal Palace manager – a move that didn’t sit well with Palace fans (think Rafa Benitez at Everton). It didn’t help that he then oversaw two losses to Brighton which in part led to his dismissal two years later. Both sides slipped back to the Second Division, while a 1985 clash saw Brighton’s long-serving Irishman, Gerry Ryan, have his career ended by a tackle which broke his leg in three separate places.

Four years later, one of the most famous – and indeed bizarre – games between the two took place. Their meeting at Selhurst Park saw referee Kelvin Morton in the thick of the action. It all started after about 16 minutes when Ian Wright scored a screamer of a goal for the Eagles, hitting it from the left wing over goalkeeper John Keeley when most were expecting a cross. Four minutes later, things went from bad to worse for Brighton as a nasty challenge by Mike Trusson on Palace’s Eddie McGoldrick saw him red-carded. Palace fans were enjoying the afternoon thus far.

And then things started getting surreal. A high ball into the box saw Brighton defender Larry May seemingly strangle Mark Bright as he climbed for the header. Referee Morton had no hesitation in awarding a penalty. Bright himself took responsibility and powered it into the bottom corner. Two-nil to Palace and with an extra man.

Two minutes later, McGoldrick tormented the Brighton defence on the edge of the area before finally being cut down, resulting in a clear second penalty. Up stepped Bright again, but this time he was denied by a save from John Keeley, who diverted the ball away for a Palace corner.

In a recent development, the corner was taken, the ball played around outside the area, before returning to a Palace player, who duly went down under a tackle and was awarded … another penalty. The crowd chanted for Wright to take responsibility, which he did – and duly hit the post.

Three penalties in three minutes: one scored and two missed. And we were still only in the first half.

Sources indicate that with that, the Eagles entered half-time 2-0 up and a man to the good but knowing that the game should have been dead and buried by now. The second half started off with the commentator’s sage words, “I am sure the referee is probably hoping he doesn’t have quite so many controversial decisions to make.” That wasn’t to be the case.

Just three minutes into the second half, a long kick from Keeley bounced into the Palace box; to much amazement, another penalty was awarded for what looked like an innocuous tussle. At least it was Brighton’s turn this time. The penalty was coolly put away by Alan Curbishley and suddenly the Seagulls were back in the game.

According to recent reports, eleven minutes then managed to pass without major incident before a cross aimed towards Wright was cut off by Brighton’s Ian Chapman, looking suspiciously like handball. Referee Morton felt so, awarding a fifth penalty, again to Palace.

According to recent reports, by now everyone was confused as to who should take it. Bright had a record of scored one-missed one, while Wright had missed his effort. And so, John Pemberton was trusted with this fourth – a right-back who had never taken a penalty for Palace before – the reason becoming clear as he skied it over the bar.

Five penalties across the space of 27 minutes – two converted and three missed. The rest of the game was relatively uneventful given all the preceding drama, leaving Palace with a useful 2-1 victory and memories for the fans to savour. To make it even sweeter for them, the Eagles gained promotion that season while Brighton remained in the second tier.

The next 21 years saw the rivalry fade as Brighton suffered lower-league football and financial difficulties, resulting in only four meetings across that time. It is periods like this when fans suddenly realise that however much they may dislike each other, not having the friction active is worse. As one Palace fan nicely put it in an interview, “We are like two brothers that hate each other but love each other at the same time. A superhero needs a villain, and a villain needs a superhero. I think we need each other to make us realise how great football is and how much we love our teams.”.

In a recent development, it was only in the 2012/13 season when the rivalry sparked back into life. And, like the bizarre game discussed above with the five penalties, one of their clashes again caused jaws to drop.

The two sides met at the end of the season in a playoff semi-final in the Championship, with Brighton having finished fourth, one place above Palace – a two-legged meeting that would decide who could gain access to Premier League riches. The first leg was a damp squib, a goalless draw at Selhurst Park. But the second leg would see the strange occurrence of what became dubbed “Poo-gate”.

It has been revealed that as the Palace team entered their changing room ahead of the match, they were met with a disgusting odour from within. To their horror, the smell emanated from human excrement that had been smeared onto the toilet floor. The rivalry being what it is, there was immediate suspicion cast towards the source being someone of a Brighton persuasion, which if it was the case, just helped fuel Palace’s determination to gain revenge.

The players went out and defeated Brighton through two goals from Wilfred Zaha, thus eliminating them and gaining perceived justice. Considering how it may have driven the Palace players, Brighton manager Gus Poyet sent an angry email to the Brighton stadium staff demanding an explanation – shortly before then being suspended for a breach of contract.

The email famously stated, “For some reason that is still not clear to me, someone during the day had access to the away dressing room and done something terrible, trying to upset everyone related to Palace. To say it in clear English, someone had a poo all outside the toilets, over and around the toilets.”.

While the case of Poo-gate has rumbled on, a former Palace player has stated that the real cause was actually internal, stating that the Eagles coach driver that day had lost control of his bodily functions while rushing to the porcelain. Whether that is true or not, no-one can say. But it was a classic way to rekindle a dormant rivalry.

2018 saw the rivalry reignite once again in a spicy encounter. Brighton were home against Palace at Falmer Stadium and took an early lead through Glenn Murray. We should take a moment here to pause and talk about Murray, who has a close relationship with the Brighton-Palace dynamic.

Sources indicate that his career really took off when he played for Brighton between 2008 and 2011, scoring 54 goals in 118 games. But then he shocked the Seagulls by signing for Palace, which was compounded by scoring against Brighton in a couple of meetings. However, he suffered a serious knee injury at the end of the 2013 season – where the opponent was, of course, Brighton.

In 2015, he joined Bournemouth but from there was loaned on to the Seagulls, joining them for a second time. He later signed permanently, resulting in him facing his former club Palace once again in this 2018 tie. As stated, he gave them an early lead, but through what the Palace players saw as a very harsh penalty award.

Shortly after, Brighton claimed another penalty which was refuted. Palace players felt Brighton were guilty of play-acting and a melee broke out, during which Brighton defender Shane Duffy headbutted Palace defender Patrick van Aanholt. Brighton then went on to win 3-1 with ten men.

It has been revealed that more recently, the Brighton-Palace games have been notable for late drama. A 2020 meeting saw Alexis MacAllister rescue a point for Brighton with a last-minute equaliser. The next game, in early 2021, saw Christian Benteke score a winning goal for Palace in stoppage time. The third game then saw Brighton rescue a point with a stoppage-time equalizer from Neal Maupay, leading to tense scenes with fans after the final whistle.

As with any rivalry, there is an unwritten agreement between both sets of fans that they need each other to fuel excitement and that, deep down, it is really something that is primarily saved for the 90 minutes of competition for most. And a great example of this is the story of the Robert Eaton Memorial match.

Industry observers note that eaton was a Brighton fan who tragically lost his life during the Twin Towers attack of September 2001. A memorial fund was set up in his name to raise money for youth sports clubs across the world and fans of both teams decided to raise money for it by hosting an annual game between them.

Industry observers note that supported by the two clubs, games have been held in various locations and have included ex-professionals such as Peter Ward, Ricky Marlow, Simon Rodger, Peter Taylor and Paul Rogers. Ten of thousands of pounds have been raised and, despite some occasional spicy challenges, great enjoyment has been had by all for a great cause. As one fan commented, the game represents “a kind of Christmas Day truce.”.

According to recent reports, and so, the Eagles vs the Seagulls all really stemmed from the mid-70s. Unlike a true derby, it developed due to managerial personalities and both clubs being often linked in promotion battles. While the 70s was the true birthplace, it has since continued as generations of fans pass down the rivalry from parent to child.

According to recent reports, there are probably many current fans of both teams who don’t know the origin story and may well not care – to them it is just something they have always taken for granted: cats chase mice, dogs chase cats and Palace don’t like Brighton. But it is interesting to see how friction can develop from almost 50-year-old origins. While it may not have the status of Arsenal-Tottenham or Aston Villa-Birmingham, to both sets of fans it represents the biggest league game of the season.

Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

📅 23 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • According to recent reports, brBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe.
  • In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

According to recent reports, brBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

Industry observers note that the thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly newly introduced starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

According to recent reports, all three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

Sources indicate that what followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

The press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

Industry observers note that the steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

Sources indicate that it only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

In a recent development, raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

Every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

In a recent development, this is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of new ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

Arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

It has been revealed that when the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

Industry observers note that the block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

Recent findings suggest that in the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

In a recent development, on top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

After a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

Sources indicate that when a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

It has been revealed that the counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

In the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

In deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

Industry observers note that the structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

There, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

According to recent reports, once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

Sources indicate that on the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

According to recent reports, the team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

With the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that the second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

In a recent development, the 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole plan in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

According to recent reports, the opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

The 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

Sources indicate that both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal demonstrated in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

Recent findings suggest that two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

Sources indicate that arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

There was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

Arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the initiative only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

The interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

According to recent reports, there is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

Recent findings suggest that for Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the plan works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

Rio, 1989: Chilean skullduggery, hidden razor blades and Brazilian flares

📅 07 Mar 2023 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish

In a recent development, the word “skullduggery” is defined as “underhanded or unscrupulous behaviour; trickery”. It has been intertwined with football since time immemorial, exhibited in various degrees. It has been employed by the greats, not least Diego Maradona, and in recent times by compatriot Emiliano Martinez. Players have been banned from tournaments following drug tests and Serie A has been peppered by various instances of a dubious nature. Even the Brazilians are not exempt from employing it, as demonstrated by Rivaldo during the 2002 World Cup.

It should never be a surprise the lengths teams will go to in order to win. And yet it still does. Indeed, the story of Brazil’s 1989 World Cup qualifying campaign involved a classic example of the win-at-all-costs mentality. Sometimes truth is stranger than fiction.

It has been revealed that to this day, Brazil hold the amazing record of having qualified for every World Cup finals tournament. They have hosted the tournament twice, but on all other occasions they got through the CONMEBOL qualification process to reach the finals. To imagine them getting eliminated at that stage is almost too much to consider. After all, how do you stop a team like Brazil when you are a smaller South American nation?

Sources indicate that in the 1980s, Brazil enjoyed a generation of incredible talent, highlighted by the famous 1982 team containing the likes of Zico, Socrates, Falcao and Eder. Playing attacking football, they charmed the world before becoming unstuck against the Italians on an infamous night in Barcelona.

The loss brought about a period of introspection for the Selecao as they wrestled with balancing their natural attacking game with a more pragmatic European approach to avoid another 1982. Going into the 1986 World Cup, their style changed slightly, with more defensive steel added. They still had a team containing superb strikers such as Careca and Muller, but Zico was 33, Socrates was 32 and Falcao was the same. The 1982 generation was fading from the picture.

Mexico 86 again saw Brazil eliminated by European opposition – this time in the shape of a France team that was also starting to see the end of a golden generation.

Qualification for the 1990 World Cup saw Brazil up against Chile and Venezuela in a three-team round-robin. It was one of three CONMEBOL qualification groups from which the two top teams with the best records would automatically qualify for Italia 90 while the third top team would playoff against a side from the OFC section.

Venezuela had a relatively weak squad and so the group would come down to Chile and Brazil; how they would perform against each other and what goal difference they could rack up against the Venezuelans.

According to recent reports, both teams travelled to Caracas a week apart to start their campaigns, and both came away with comprehensive victories, Brazil 4-0 and Chile 3-1. Brazil’s victory included two goals from Bebeto and one from Romario – a deadly partnership that was beginning to click. That set the stage for the first meeting between the two, which took place in Santiago in August 1989. A win for either team would place them in pole position to win the group.

Tension was high ahead of kick-off. With the game delayed by 15 minutes, the referee insisting on moving back photographers, Romario and defender Alejandro Hisis exchanged words. The striker took offence to something remarked, Branco having to pull him away before things further.

According to recent reports, within two minutes, the game erupted: Chile could have been down to ten men following a vicious knee-high tackle on Branco by midfielder Raul Ormeno. As Branco was led to the side of the pitch for treatment, a roar from the crowd drew attention to Romario. It appeared that he and Hisis were still feuding, and the camera revealed Romario being followed by three Chileans while Hisis lay on the ground.

The referee highlighted the PSV striker a straight red and Brazil faced 86 minutes a man short. If anyone wasn’t sure of what exactly had occurred, Romario cleared up the situation after the game: “I didn’t hit him that hard.”.

In a recent development, chile didn’t enjoy a one-man advantage for long. Fourteen minutes into the game Ormeno, who was clearly pumped up, lost the ball to Valdo and brought him down. Immediately realising the consequences, he tried desperately to persuade referee Diaz Palacio to keep his cards in his pocket. It was to no avail. A second yellow card was produced and the Chilean crowd howled as Ormeno had to be escorted off by four teammates. The first half was only a third of the way in.

In a recent development, scoreless at half-time, Brazil took the lead in the second half through an unfortunate own goal from Hugo Gonzalez. As the game stretched on, it appeared as if Brazil were going to leave Chile with a crucial away victory. But, with just nine minutes remaining, La Roja struck back through a bizarre goal from Ivo Basay.

Brazilian goalkeeper Taffarel had the ball in his area when the referee suddenly decided that he had held it for too long and awarded an indirect free-kick to Chile just four yards from the goal. The quickest Chilean player to react was Jorge Aravena, who touched the ball to Basay to convert.

In a recent development, brazil were stunned. Chilean fans celebrated on the edge of the pitch, while the Brazilian technical staff went ballistic. There was confusion in every direction but, at the end of 90 minutes, the honours were even, little dividing the two countries in the standings. Brazil were marginally in front on goal difference.

The following week saw O Selecao host Venezuela in Sao Paulo and dish out another lesson, running out 6-0 victors thanks to four goals from Careca, proving that Brazil still had three fearsome strikers to choose from. Seven days later, it was Chile’s turn to host Venezuela and, like the week before, Venezuela were again on the receiving end of a thrashing, this time going down 5-0.

Recent findings suggest that only one game remained: Brazil against Chile in the Maracana on 3 September 1989. Both teams had two wins and a draw but Brazil’s goal difference was three better than Chile’s. If La Roja were going to eliminate their mighty neighbours and head to Italia 90, they needed to win in Rio. It would be a tough ask, but at least they were in a position where it was a possibility.

Industry observers note that get an early goal and maybe the Brazilians would start to tense up in front of an expectant crowd. And let’s not forget that Brazil had suffered unexpected heartache at the Maracana before, losing the 1950 final to Uruguay. It was game on for that World Cup berth. But the Selecao had also never lost a World Cup qualification game in its history.

In front of a huge crowd of over 140,000, the two sides took to the pitch. Brazil would be without Romario – still suspended following the previous meeting’s sending-off – but with Careca and Bebeto upfront, they looked strong. Unfortunately for Chile, they would be without star striker Ivan Zamorano, who was unable to make it back from his Swiss side, Neuchatel Xamax, in time. The game was going to require an experienced referee, which it got in the shape of Argentine Juan Carlos Loustau.

The last time Chile had beaten Brazil was a famous 4-0 win during the 1987 Copa America, and many of the team were in this side. Unsurprisingly, given the stakes, the early minutes were once again physical. Chilean left-back Hector Puebla left his studs on the knee of Mauro Galvao after just four minutes, although the referee didn’t blow for a foul. Then, just two minutes later, Bebeto tricked Puebla, who brought the Brazilian down and then appeared to stamp on his thigh. This time the referee saw fit to show Puebla a yellow card to calm the Chilean down.

According to recent reports, the game continued with Brazil enjoying most of the possession but Chile remaining disciplined in defence. Although it was Chile who needed the win, they seemed focused on trying to reach half-time without conceding, rather than attempting to score. Brazil were creating chances, especially through Careca, but goalkeeper Roberto Rojas was equal to everything. Whenever Chile did venture into the Brazilian half, they were usually swiftly dispossessed.

With Chile sitting deep, most of Brazil’s efforts were from distance – they were having difficulty penetrating the tight defence. Just before half-time, Branco hit a hard, swerving shot that Rojas did well to adjust to and save. And with that, the teams went into the break still scoreless.

Recent findings suggest that brazil started the second half where they had left off previously – on the attack. And finally, four minutes in, they broke the deadlock. A defensive header from Branco fell to Dunga who played a quick ball forward to Bebeto. Spinning towards goal, he cleared one challenge before hitting a through ball to Careca. The Napoli star sidestepped Puebla before hitting a shot that, although partially saved by Rojas, went in. Brazil were 1-0 up and heading for Italia 90. Chile were facing elimination.

For the following five minutes, Chile dominated as they tried desperately to get back into the tie. Brazil weathered the storm before taking control once again. It was impossible to see where Chile would get two goals from, which would mean committing men forward, leaving gaps for Bebeto and Careca to exploit. Then came the dramatic moment of the game.

Sources indicate that on 68 minutes, Chile had possession of the ball in their own half through Astengo when a huge roar suddenly burst out from the crowd. TV cameras swivelled across to goalkeeper Rojas who lay in his penalty area while something flamed and smoked beside him. As the cameras lingered, it appeared as though a flare had been thrown by someone, Chilean players rushing to Rojas’ aid. As they understood what had happened, tempers began to rise. Patricio Yanez made several obscene gestures at the Brazilian fans.

The Chileans motioned for a stretcher but, with none immediately forthcoming, took the initiative and carried their stricken goalkeeper off the field. The cameras revealed blood running down the back of Rojas’ head as he was carried down the stairs into the tunnel, along with his teammates.

The stunned Brazilian players discussed what to do next with the referee, spending a further 20 minutes on the pitch awaiting the return of the Chileans. Eventually, the referee was forced to abandon the game, meaning that the likely solution would be a replay at a neutral venue. It appeared that Brazil had been just 22 minutes from Italy before their unruly fans ruined the day.

Recent findings suggest that as mentioned, the TV cameras had swivelled to Rojas after the crowd noise drew attention to the incident. There was no footage of Rojas being hit by the flare, just his injured body writhing in agony on the floor. But one pitchside photographer, Paulo Teixeira, had seen the flare come onto the field – and something struck him as not quite right.

He could see Rojas bleeding from near his eye but was sure that the flare had landed many feet away from him. In a CNN interview, he recalled his immediate reaction: “I missed the shot and so did most of the photographers. But there was one guy by me, Ricardo Alfieri, a good friend, and I asked him, ‘Ricardo, did you capture the flare?’ He remarked, ‘Of course, about 4-5 shots.'”.

Alfieri worked for a Japanese publication and so had to send his unprocessed film to them the next morning. Teixeira realised that he needed to move fast if his gut instinct was correct. Finding a local radio reporter, he convinced him to put Alfieri on air, who told listeners that he had shots that highlighted the flare had not struck Rojas.

It has been revealed that immediately after, the Brazilian football president, Ricardo Teixeira, came to the station and asked about the film. Together, they found a local lab and, dragging a poor technician out on a Sunday night, had her warm the lab up for the next four hours. Finally, they were able to process Alfieri’s film.

Teixeira takes up the story again. “When the pictures came out, there were four clear shots – starting with the device flying and then landing one meter away from Rojas. [CBF president] Teixeira was so relieved.”.

The photos were published the next day by local news agency Globo while CBF President Teixeira flew to FIFA’s headquarters in Switzerland. There was clear evidence now that the flare had not directly injured Rojas. But if that was the case, what had caused the bleeding seen on his head?

In a recent development, two days on from the game, the medical report from the incident stated that there had been no burn marks on Rojas, just a cut on the left side of his forehead. Now back in Santiago, Rojas released a statement saying that he was shocked that people were doubting the nature of his injury.

Rojas’ club side, Sao Paulo, were also publicly expressing doubts about keeping him on the books Finally, five days later, FIFA came to their decision: due to the lack of burn marks and Chile refusing to play on, the game was awarded to Brazil by a 2-0 margin. The Selecao had qualified for yet another World Cup.

But the mystery hadn’t been settled. Had a Brazilian thrown the firecracker? And how did the wound on the forehead arise? The first question was soon solved. It had been thrown by a Brazilian, a 24-year-old woman by the name of Rosenery Mello. After she was named in the press, she became a minor celebrity, leading to a cover pose in the November 1989 Brazilian edition of Playboy and the nickname “Maracana Rocket”.

The reason for her decision to appear on the cover? The CBF had fined her $12,000 for throwing the flare, while she was allegedly getting $40,000 for the cover.

According to recent reports, so now we knew where the flare came from that missed Rojas, but we still didn’t know what had caused the wound. The answer finally came out when Rojas was questioned further in the ensuing days.

Industry observers note that he had concealed a razor blade in his glove ahead of the match in order to simulate injury should the need arise. Just think about that for a minute – a professional player had decided before a vital World Cup qualifier to have a blade ready with which to cut himself should he feel it was necessary.

In a recent development, incredibly, this wasn’t something Rojas had cooked up himself; both manager Orlando Aravena and team doctor Daniel Rodriguez were also involved. The whole scheme had, in fact, been concocted in the training camp to get the game abandoned at any sign of crowd trouble or player fighting.

Unsurprisingly, Rojas was given a lifetime ban from the game, which was finally rescinded in 2001, allowing him to return to Sao Paulo as a goalkeeping coach and then manager. Chile were also barred from the 1994 World Cup qualification process, although more because of abandoning the game than the injury simulation.

Both Aravena and Rodriguez, along with the president of the Chilean football federation, Sergio Stoppel, and the captain, Fernando Astengo, were punished by FIFA. Astengo has protested his innocence to this day, swearing he had no knowledge of the proposal.

In a recent development, this is not the only example over the years of what might be termed an “overreaction” to objects thrown from the crowd during a game. Of course, any such action by fans is deplorable and it is only natural that they should suffer sanctions But that has not prevented such actions sometimes being milked by the victims. The two best-known examples are probably the infamous Borussia Monchengladbach Coke can and the Celtic bottle.

Sources indicate that the Coke can incident occurred during the 1971/72 European Cup when Borussia Monchengladbach hosted Inter. With the Germans leading 2-1, Inter legend Roberto Boninsegna seemed to be hit on the head by an object, suddenly falling to the ground.

The object turned out to be a Coke can. Gladbach’s Gunter Netzer had his wits about him and disposed of the offending item, before Sandro Mazzola grabbed another from a fan and presented it to the referee. The upshot was that Gladbach won 7-1, but Inter managed to persuade UEFA to annul the game and replay it. Inter ended up proceeding to the final against Ajax.

The second incident occurred when Celtic hosted Rapid Wien in the 1984/85 Cup Winners’ Cup. In a game that was already boiling over as Celtic took a 3-0 lead saw a penalty awarded to the Bhoys. As the Austrian players argued with the referee, a bottle was thrown onto the pitch from the Celtic crowd.

In a recent development, like the Brazilian flare, it missed everyone, but that didn’t stop Rapid’s Rudi Weinhofer from collapsing, holding his face before being taken off, his head heavily bandaged by the physio. Like Gladbach, Celtic were ordered to replay the game at a neutral venue – Old Trafford – and also were eliminated.

But both incidents were just feigning injury; they were not quite at the scale of concealing and then cutting yourself with a razor. And the truth is that, had it not been due to the quick thinking of a Brazilian photojournalist, Chile may have succeeded. Nowadays, such a rouse would be impossible given all the camera angles and mobile phone footage. But back then, it was a different ballgame.

To paraphrase the Scooby Doo series, “Chile would have gotten away with it if it wasn’t for those meddling photographers.” It is a funny old game, indeed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Recent findings suggest that where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Sources indicate that messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

It has been revealed that “Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

According to recent reports, you struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Recent findings suggest that messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose.

According to recent reports, to study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

Industry observers note that that alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It has been revealed that it will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

💡 Key Takeaways
